answer: Amber reached its highest value in the 4th millennium BCE (peak Z-amber = 1.54, attained in three century-bins at 3300, 3200 and 3100 BCE). The peak interval is a 400-year plateau from 3300 BCE to 2900 BCE — four consecutive century-bins tied at Z-amber = 1.54, of which three sit inside the 4th millennium BCE and one (3000 BCE, group MN) opens the 3rd millennium BCE under the ISO millennium convention. Both time_series_data.Amber and capital.Zamber agree on the value, the four centuries and the millennium placement.

payload.hypothesis: Amber reached its highest value in the 4th millennium BCE (Z-amber = 1.54, recorded at 3300, 3200 and 3100 BCE), and the peak interval is a 400-year plateau from 3300 BCE to 2900 BCE — four consecutive century-bins holding Z-amber = 1.54, of which three sit inside the 4th millennium BCE and one (3000 BCE) opens the 3rd millennium BCE under the ISO millennium boundary convention.
payload.workflow: Load time_series_data.csv (raw Amber; Amber_inter for plateau-shape cross-check) and capital.csv (Zamber; comma-decimal European format). Build ISO-standard right-open millennium bins (4th millennium BCE = CE -4000 .. -3001; CE -3000 -> 3rd millennium BCE). Per millennium, aggregate raw Z-amber by max (headline), count@max (tiebreak-1), mean (tiebreak-2). Confirm: raw Amber=1.54 at CE -3300, -3200, -3100, -3000 (calBP 5250, 5150, 5050, 4950). Both Amber and Zamber agree everywhere they overlap. Amber_inter is flat at 1.5400 across the entire peak window CE -3300 .. -2900, ruling out any thin-bin spike. Peak millennium = 4th millennium BCE (3 bins at max, mean 1.484); peak interval = 3300 BCE .. 2900 BCE inclusive (400 years).
